games.title: Space Panic
games.note: The first game built around climbing ladders between floors of platforms.

games.title: Jump Bug
games.note: The first platform game with horizontal and, in one stretch, vertical scrolling.

games.title: Pitfall!
games.note: Sold over 4 million copies on the Atari 2600, one of the console's best sellers.

games.title: Pitfall II: Lost Caverns
games.note: One of the largest Atari 2600 games; its cartridge carried an extra chip for richer music.

games.title: Adventure
games.note: Robinett hid his own name in a secret room, an early video game Easter egg.

games.title: Radar Scope
games.note: Its unsold US cabinets were converted into Donkey Kong machines.

games.title: Donkey Kong Jr.
games.note: Mario is the villain here, holding Donkey Kong captive.

games.title: Excitebike
games.note: Its fast side-scrolling engine was reused for Super Mario Bros.

games.title: Pac-Land
games.note: An early scrolling platformer starring Pac-Man, styled after his cartoon series.

games.title: Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels
games.note: Japan's Super Mario Bros. 2; judged too hard for the West, it only came out there in 1993.

games.title: Doki Doki Panic
games.note: Made with Fuji TV; Nintendo reskinned it as the Western Super Mario Bros. 2.

games.title: Super Mario Bros. 2
games.note: Brought Shy Guys, Bob-ombs and Birdo into the Mario series.

games.title: Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins
games.note: The debut of Wario, who got his own series two years later.

games.title: Mario Paint
games.note: Shipped with the SNES Mouse; its music maker still has a fan following.

games.title: Super Mario Maker
games.note: Began as an internal Nintendo tool for building Mario levels.

games.title: Donkey Kong Jungle Beat
games.note: Played with the DK Bongos drum controller.

games.title: Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest
Kirby's Adventure
games.note: The first Kirby game where he copies enemies' powers. Directed by Masahiro Sakurai.

games.title: Sonic CD
games.note: Sonic travels to past and future versions of each zone.

games.title: Sonic Mania
games.note: Built on Christian Whitehead's Retro Engine, with art and levels by PagodaWest and Headcannon.

games.title: Jazz Jackrabbit
games.note: Designed by Cliff Bleszinski, later lead designer of Gears of War.

games.title: Earthworm Jim
games.note: Made as a satire of the platform games of its day; created by Doug TenNapel.

games.title: Commander Keen
games.note: Invasion of the Vorticons; John Carmack's adaptive tile refresh gave PCs smooth console-style scrolling.

games.title: Wonder Boy
games.note: Designed by Ryuichi Nishizawa; Hudson Soft adapted it as Adventure Island.

games.title: Adventure Island
games.note: Its hero is modeled on Hudson's spokesman Takahashi Meijin.

games.title: Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap
games.note: A curse turns the hero into different animals, each opening new paths.

games.title: Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap
games.note: You can switch between new hand-drawn art and the 1989 graphics at any time.

games.title: Alex Kidd in Miracle World
games.note: Boss fights are settled with rock-paper-scissors.

games.title: The Great Giana Sisters
games.note: Pulled from sale in 1988 after Nintendo objected to its likeness to Super Mario Bros.

games.title: Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams
games.note: Swaps each level between a cute dream and a nightmare version.

games.title: Mega Man 9
games.note: Deliberately made with NES-style 8-bit graphics and sound in 2008.

games.title: Rayman 2: The Great Escape
games.note: Took Michel Ancel's limbless hero into 3D.

links.took: Floors of platforms joined by ladders, the layout historians call the genre's foundation.
links.added: Jumping, a cast of characters and a story told across four distinct screens.
links.extra: No Nintendo statement links them; a historian quoted by Wikipedia calls Space Panic the foundation of all platformers.

links.took: Digging holes in the floor to trap chasing enemies.
links.added: Gold to collect, 150 puzzle-like levels and a built-in level editor.

links.took: The ladders-and-platforms layout; creator Nigel Alderton cites Space Panic as a particular inspiration.
links.added: A farm of eggs and grain to collect, with roaming hens and a caged giant duck.

links.took: Nearly everything: it was an unauthorized home version of Space Panic's digging and climbing.
links.added: Brought the idea to the Apple II, where it became a top seller.
links.extra: Over a dozen Space Panic clones appeared on home systems, often with 'panic' in the name.

links.took: Its cabinets and circuit board: about 2,000 unsold Radar Scope machines were converted.
links.added: A new game by first-time lead designer Shigeru Miyamoto, supervised by Gunpei Yokoi.
links.extra: Radar Scope flopped in the US, leaving Nintendo of America with unsold cabinets to salvage.

links.took: Donkey Kong, Mario and single-screen climbing stages.
links.added: Climbing vines and chains as DK's son, with Mario as the villain.

links.took: Single-screen platforms, ladders and jumping, from the wave of games after Donkey Kong.
links.added: Claiming every platform by walking over it, across a series of mine stations.

links.took: Its hero's name, the original name for Mario in Donkey Kong.
links.added: Thirty levels of bomb defusing on girders and ladders for home computers.

links.took: Mario himself, plus stage parts such as lifts and ladders that the team imported from Donkey Kong.
links.added: One long scrolling journey through eight worlds instead of single-screen stages.

links.took: Ropes, logs and springs, which the team imported from Donkey Kong Jr.
links.added: Used them as obstacles across a scrolling world with power-ups.

links.took: The fast side-scrolling engine Miyamoto's team first built for Excitebike.
links.added: Smooth scrolling across large worlds full of secrets, warp pipes and power-ups.

links.took: Side-scrolling know-how; Nintendo's Kung Fu port was a step toward Miyamoto's scrolling platformer.
links.added: Jumping and exploring instead of punching down a single corridor.
links.extra: Nintendo made Kung Fu, its port of Irem's arcade game, months before Super Mario Bros.

links.took: A scrolling platformer with a cartoon hero jumping over hazards on the way to a goal.
links.added: Joystick control, power-ups, hidden secrets and eight worlds of varied stages.
links.extra: Wikipedia names Pac-Land as an influence on Super Mario Bros.

links.took: Running and jumping past pits, hazards and creatures, the formula Pitfall! popularized at home.
links.added: Scrolling worlds, power-ups and enemies you defeat by stomping.
links.extra: GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann said Pitfall! launched the platformer genre as we know it. No Nintendo statement links the two.

links.took: Pitfall Harry, jungle hazards and David Crane's design.
links.added: One huge scrolling cavern with checkpoints, swimming and balloon rides.

links.took: A large world to explore on the Atari 2600, built from connected screens.
links.added: Running, jumping and swinging on vines, with a timer and treasures to grab.

src.t: Nick Montfort and Ian Bogost, Racing the Beam, via Wikipedia: Pitfall!

links.extra: Montfort and Bogost say Pitfall! built on Adventure's genre to create something like a later open-world game.

links.took: Exploring a fantasy world of screens, finding items and keys, and fighting monsters.
links.added: A much bigger overworld, dungeons, saved progress and an upgradeable hero.
links.extra: Wikipedia credits Adventure with popularizing action-adventure games on consoles. Nintendo has not named it as an influence.

links.took: Forced horizontal scrolling over terrain while shooting, as in Scramble and Super Cobra earlier in 1981.
links.added: A bouncing car that hops between platforms, the first scrolling platform game.

links.took: Collecting items across single-screen mine caverns, as in Miner 2049er.
links.added: Twenty surreal caverns, an air supply timer and in-game music on the ZX Spectrum.

links.took: The same engine, graphics and eight-world structure.
links.added: Much harder levels, wind gusts, poison mushrooms and Luigi's higher jump.

links.took: The Super Mario name and cast, applied to a reworked Doki Doki Panic.
links.added: Four playable heroes with different jumps, and plucking vegetables to throw.

links.took: Its levels, engine and mechanics; Nintendo swapped in Mario characters for the West.
links.added: Mario, Luigi, Toad and Peach as the four heroes, with reworked graphics and music.

links.took: Mario's Game Boy platforming.
links.added: A world map, saving, bigger sprites and Wario as the new villain.

src.t: Wikipedia: Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins

links.took: Wario, the villain introduced in Super Mario Land 2.
links.added: Made him the star, charging through walls and wearing hats for new powers.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wario Land: Super Mario Land 3

links.took: Creative tools for players; Takashi Tezuka first wanted a Wii U follow-up to Mario Paint.
links.added: Turned the idea into a Mario level editor with online sharing.
links.extra: Tezuka decided a course-making tool would sell better than an art program.

links.took: Its graphics and stage parts, one of four selectable styles.
links.added: Build your own courses on the GamePad and share them online.

links.took: Its graphics and stage parts, one of the four selectable Mario Maker styles.
links.added: Mixing parts freely, like stacking enemies or giving them wings.

links.took: Classic side-scrolling Mario across eight worlds.
links.added: 3D-modeled characters, Mega and Mini Mushrooms and wall jumps, the first new 2D Mario in years.

links.took: The team: Nintendo EAD Tokyo started Galaxy after Jungle Beat, with Yoshiaki Koizumi joining.
links.added: Spherical planets with their own gravity, an idea from the Super Mario 128 demo.

links.took: Its creator: Bananza's idea came from Yoshiaki Koizumi, who directed Jungle Beat.
links.added: Smashable voxel terrain that Donkey Kong punches and digs through.

links.took: Donkey Kong, bananas and jungle platforming.
links.added: Bongo drum controls, combo scoring and clapping to stun enemies.

links.took: Rare's pre-rendered 3D look, barrels, animal buddies and themed stages.
links.added: Diddy and Dixie Kong, whose spinning ponytail lets her glide.

src.t: Wikipedia: Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest

links.took: Donkey and Diddy Kong, barrel cannons, minecarts and banana hunting.
links.added: Retro Studios' revival with 2.5D graphics and two-player co-op.

links.took: Retro's revived DKC style, co-op and tough level design.
links.added: Dixie and Cranky as partners, underwater stages and a dynamic camera.

src.t: Wikipedia: Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze

links.took: Kirby, inhaling enemies, floating and Dream Land.
links.added: The Copy Ability: swallow an enemy to gain its power.

links.took: The Copy Ability, a series staple since Kirby's Adventure.
links.added: Full 3D stages in a ruined human world, and Mouthful Mode.

links.took: Mario-style platforming; Yuji Naka wondered why Super Mario Bros. levels couldn't be cleared faster.
links.added: Speed: slopes, loops and rolling, with rings that protect you from hits.

src.t: Wikipedia: Sonic the Hedgehog (1991 video game)

links.extra: Sonic's default speed was set to that of Mario while running.

links.took: Naka ported it to the Mega Drive; its slow movement pushed him to work on speed.
links.added: A fast, physics-driven hero who builds momentum on curved terrain.

src.t: Wikipedia: Sonic the Hedgehog (1991 video game)

links.extra: Naka has said that without Ghouls 'n Ghosts there would be no Sonic.

links.took: The checkered ground effect, an idea Naka got from Yu Suzuki's work on Space Harrier.
links.added: Used the checkerboard look on the slopes and loops of Green Hill Zone.

src.t: Wikipedia: Sonic the Hedgehog (1991 video game)

links.took: Sonic, rings, loops and the first game's physics.
links.added: Time travel between past, present and future versions of each zone.

links.took: Big, wide open level design, which the team cited from Sonic CD.
links.added: Remixed classic zones plus new ones, built on Christian Whitehead's Retro Engine.

links.took: Its gameplay model and streamlined level design, which the team said they followed.
links.added: A new Drop Dash move and fresh hand-drawn sprite art in the 16-bit style.

links.took: Fast, colorful mascot platforming; it was first seen as a PC take on Sonic.
links.added: A gun-toting rabbit, shareware episodes and fast scrolling on DOS PCs.

links.took: Speedy Amiga mascot platforming, which Wikipedia credits as a major influence.
links.added: Brought that style to DOS with a rabbit hero and weapons.

links.took: The mascot-platformer moment; publisher Playmates wanted a game-first franchise after Sonic's success.
links.added: A super-suited worm, hand-animated gags and a satire of platform game cliches.

src.t: Wikipedia: Sonic the Hedgehog (1991 video game)

links.extra: Wikipedia lists Earthworm Jim among the mascot platformers that followed Sonic.

links.took: A fast animal mascot with attitude, one of many that followed Sonic.
links.added: A wisecracking bobcat who glides across wide, open levels.

src.t: Wikipedia: Sonic the Hedgehog (1991 video game)

links.took: A wisecracking animal mascot; Gex's makers cite Sonic as a major inspiration.
links.added: A TV-obsessed gecko who climbs walls through television-themed worlds.

src.t: Wikipedia: Sonic the Hedgehog (1991 video game)

links.took: Smooth console-style scrolling; the team first cloned Super Mario Bros. 3's opening level on PC.
links.added: An original hero, a boy genius with a pogo stick, sold as shareware episodes.

src.t: Wikipedia: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons

links.extra: The demo was called Dangerous Dave in Copyright Infringement.

links.took: Tom Hall's design brief: a console-style platformer in the vein of Super Mario Bros.
links.added: A Chuck Jones-flavored sci-fi kid hero, alien worlds and a pogo stick.

src.t: Wikipedia: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons

links.took: Side-scrolling run-and-jump through cartoon scenery; Wikipedia calls Pac-Land the common ancestor of Wonder Boy and Mario.
links.added: A food meter that drains as you run, plus skateboards and stone hatchets.

links.took: Its arcade design, adapted by Hudson Soft under license.
links.added: A new hero based on Hudson's Takahashi Meijin, and its own separate sequels.
links.extra: Adventure Island is based on the arcade version, so it contains none of the original levels.

links.took: The Wonder Boy hero, fantasy setting and Westone's team.
links.added: An interconnected world where curses turn you into animals with different abilities.

links.took: The 1989 game's map, design and animal transformations, as a faithful remake.
links.added: Hand-drawn art and a remastered soundtrack you can toggle against the originals.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap

links.took: Side-scrolling console platforming, which Super Mario Bros. popularized a year earlier.
links.added: Punching blocks and foes, vehicles, a shop and rock-paper-scissors boss matches.
links.extra: No developer statement links them; Alex Kidd was Sega's console mascot before Sonic.

links.took: Nearly everything: Manfred Trenz and Armin Gessert were asked for a game similar to Super Mario Bros.
links.added: A dream-world theme, home computer versions and a Chris Huelsbeck soundtrack.
links.extra: Nintendo objected, and the British distributor withdrew it from sale in 1988.

links.took: Giana, her sister Maria and Huelsbeck's music, newly arranged.
links.added: Switching each level between a cute dream world and a nightmare version.

links.took: Designer Manfred Trenz, who co-designed Giana Sisters before creating Turrican.
links.added: Huge explorable levels, heavy weapons and a morphing ball form.

links.took: Mega Man 2's 8-bit look, sound and structure, deliberately recreated.
links.added: A 2008 retro revival sold as a download, with tough new stages.

links.took: Rayman, his floating hands and feet, and Michel Ancel's whimsical world.
links.added: A full 3D adventure with a darker story about pirates.
